blocks.text: From safe to risky. In UI built from API data, stay left of `!`.
A **widget** is an immutable description of a piece of UI. Flutter builds the screen as a **tree** of widgets, and each widget says "draw me like this, with these children."

A widget is a **Lego instruction card**. It is not the brick itself. Flutter reads the cards and builds the real bricks, which are called elements and render objects. To change the model, you hand Flutter a new card. You never glue the old brick.

blocks.code:
primaryTextButton: LumenButton(
  label: Strings().cancel,
  semantic: SemanticsStrings().cancelButton,
  variant: LumenButtonVariant.solid,
  buttonIntent: LumenButtonIntent.brand,
  onPressed: () { CustomNavigationHelper.popTopMostPage(); },
),

blocks.text: This is a LumenButton widget. It gets a label from `Strings()`, a style (solid, brand) and a tap action. It doesn't paint anything itself. It describes, and Flutter paints.

Each widget has a `build()` method that returns more widgets. Flutter calls `build` from the root down and gets a tree. When data changes, Flutter calls `build` again for the part that changed. It compares the new tree with the old one and repaints only the differences. Rebuilding is cheap, so code that "rebuilds a lot" is normal.
Rule of thumb: inputs go in the constructor, UI goes in `build`, and actions are callbacks like `onPressed`.
A page's `build` returns a tree. Parents hold children, and leaf widgets like Text and LumenButton are what you see.

A **StatelessWidget** depends only on its inputs. A **StatefulWidget** owns a `State` object that lives across rebuilds. Calling `setState(() { … })` changes that state and asks Flutter to run `build` again.

A printed price label is stateless: same input, same label. A shop's digital counter is stateful: it remembers a number, and pressing the button (`setState`) changes the number and refreshes the display.

`setState(` appears about **604 times in 185 files**, so it is the most common state tool in the app. It is used for local, one-widget state like "is this expanded" or "selected tab". State that is shared between widgets goes into a BLoC or a ValueNotifier instead (chapters 14–16).

A StatefulWidget is a pair: the widget (config) and its State (memory). Flutter keeps the State alive even though the widget is recreated on every parent rebuild. `initState` runs once when it appears, `dispose` runs once when it leaves, and `setState` marks it dirty so `build` runs on the next frame.
Ask: does only this widget care about the value? Then use setState. Do other widgets or the API care? Then use a bloc or a notifier.
A State object's life. Only `build` repeats; `setState` sends you back to it.

**BuildContext** is a widget's address in the tree. An **InheritedWidget** (or an `InheritedModel`) puts data high up, so that any widget below can read it with `X.of(context)` and rebuild when it changes.

The building's notice board. Every flat (widget) can read the board on its floor's stairs without being told. An InheritedModel is a board with sections. You subscribe only to "water supply", so a change in "parking" doesn't knock on your door.

class GlobalPageData extends InheritedModel<Aspect> { … }   // global_page_data.dart:442
enum Aspect { bottomBar, floatingBasketButton, superSaverOaWidget,
  pdAddToBasket, basketCheckOut, totalHeight, bottomSheet, … }  // :428

GlobalPageData.of(context, aspect: Aspect.floatingBasketButton); // :505

blocks.text: The whole app shares page-level UI facts through it: bottom bar visibility, floating basket, sheet state and margins. `updateShouldNotifyDependent` (:524) decides which aspect's listeners rebuild. Code outside widgets reaches it through `CustomNavigationHelper.getGlobalData(Aspect.x)`.
The theme libraries use the same idea. `LumenThemeProvider` and `HarmonixThemeProvider` sit at the root, and every component looks up its colours through `context` (chapters 25–26).

Calling `of(context)` walks **up** the tree from your widget to the nearest provider of that type and registers you as a listener. When the provider changes, only registered listeners rebuild. With InheritedModel, only the listeners of the aspect that changed rebuild. That is why the floating basket doesn't rebuild when the bottom sheet opens.
You rarely create one; you read one:

final page = GlobalPageData.of(context, aspect: Aspect.bottomBar);
// then use page's values inside build()

blocks.text: Never store a `context` and use it later after an `await`. The widget may be gone. Check `mounted` first.
Inherited data flows down and lookups go up. The aspect makes the subscription narrow.

A **Future** is one value that arrives later, like an API response. `await` pauses the function until it arrives, without freezing the UI. A **Stream** is many values over time, like page state updates, and a `StreamBuilder` rebuilds a widget for each one.
A Future is a restaurant token: you get your food once, later. A Stream is the order-status screen at the counter: it keeps changing (preparing, ready, collected) and you keep looking at it.
One function uses both. It `await`s futures, and every `notifyDataChange()` pushes a new state into a stream.

Dart runs your code on one thread with an event loop. `await` doesn't block that thread. It parks the function and lets Flutter keep drawing frames. When the network answers, the function resumes. Errors in an awaited future surface as exceptions, so wrap them in `try/catch`. In this app `BaseApiProvider` already catches them for you (chapter 20).
`await` parks your function, not the thread. Frames keep drawing until the result returns.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Layout: how widgets get their size

blocks.text: Flutter layout follows one rule: **constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent sets the position**. A parent tells each child "you may be between these minimum and maximum sizes". The child picks a size inside that range, and the parent decides where to place it.

A bookshelf. The shelf says "you can be at most 30 cm tall" (constraint). Each book has its own height within that (size). The person filling the shelf decides the order and spacing (position). A book taller than the shelf sticks out, which is the yellow-and-black overflow stripe.

rows: Lay children out horizontally or vertically. `mainAxisAlignment` places them along the line, and `crossAxisAlignment` across it.
Share the leftover space inside a Row or Column. This is the usual fix for "RenderFlex overflowed".
Layer things, for example the floating basket over the page (`RouteAwareWidget`, 13.3)
Fixed size, gaps, decoration. In this app spacing values come from tokens, not literals (chapter 24).
Keep content out of the notch and home bar

blocks.text: When something overflows or is invisible, ask "what constraint did the parent give?". The classic cases are text in a Row without `Expanded`, a `ListView` inside a `Column` without `Expanded` (it gets unbounded height and errors), and a widget with `width: double.infinity` inside a Row.
The one layout rule. When something overflows, ask what constraint the parent gave.

`ListView.builder` builds only the rows that are on screen, which is called lazy building. **Slivers** are scrollable pieces (`SliverList`, `SliverToBoxAdapter`, `SliverAppBar`) that a `CustomScrollView` stacks into one scroll, so a header, a grid and a list scroll together.
A train whose windows only light up the carriages passing the platform (lazy building). Slivers are carriages of different shapes (a dining car, a sleeper) coupled into one train.
About 28 files use slivers. The server-driven section list (chapter 29.4) is a lazily built list, where each `index` asks `getRenderModelByPosition(index)`.

Because rows are built on demand, a section's `build` runs when it scrolls into view and is thrown away when it scrolls far out. That is why visibility-based impressions (30.4) and pagination on scroll (23.2) work, and why expensive work must not live in `build`.

For a list from data, always use `.builder` (never `ListView(children: bigList.map(...))`). Give rows that can move or change a `Key` (4.3). Inside a scroll view, never put another vertical scroll without `shrinkWrap` or a sliver.
Lazy building. It's why impressions fire on visibility and why `build` must stay cheap.

blocks.text: A **Key** tells Flutter "this is the same widget as before" when a list is reordered or rebuilt, so the right `State` stays with the right item. A **GlobalKey** is a key unique in the whole app, which also lets you reach a widget's state from outside.
Name tags at a party. Without them, if people swap seats you'd hand Ravi's drink to Asha. With tags, each drink follows its person.

A Flutter screen's life is driven by its **native view controller's** lifecycle: `viewDidLoad`, `viewWillAppear`, the first-frame callback and `deinit`. Dart learns about each step through channel calls or Flutter's `AppLifecycleListener`.

A play inside a rented hall. The hall manager (native) unlocks the hall, turns on the lights, opens the curtain and finally locks up. The actors (Dart) can only start after the curtain opens, and when the hall is locked, everything inside is cleared.

Anything else that must refresh on return has to be wired on purpose, through a lifecycle hook in the bloc (`onViewWillAppear` via `AppLifecycleListener`, `routing_page.dart:583–626`).

modules.title: Part 3: From page name to screen to CartInfoService: shared state done carefully

blocks.text: Routing uses **go_router** (14.2.6). Native, or Flutter itself, sends a `pageName`. `CustomNavigationHelper.launchPage` turns it into a **route path**. The router builds a `RouteAwareWidget` for that path, and that widget turns the page name into the real page plus its bloc. The router holds the Flutter page stack **inside one engine** (chapter 7).

A hospital. Reception (`launchPage`) hears "cardiology". The building map (the route tree) says which corridor (path) to take. On the ward, the nurse (`RouteAwareWidget`) assigns a bed and opens a patient chart (page + bloc). The bottom tabs are separate wings: switching wing keeps each wing's own rooms as they were.

Every page is registered **twice**. Under each tab it is `/<tabIndex>/<page>`, which keeps the bottom bar. At the root it is `/<page>`, which is full screen with no tabs and is used when the engine has no bottom bar. So a real location looks like `/0/productListPage/productDetailPage`: tab 0, then PL, then PD on top. Page-specific data (`pageName`, `pageId`, `pageBuilderParams`, …) is never in the path. It travels in `extra`.

blocks.text: **Harmonix** (`harmonix_library`, pinned to `release_8.44.0`, which resolves to `250603e9`) puts a `HarmonixTheme` in the tree with `package:provider`. Its `Harmonix*Component` widgets read values with `context.harmonixTheme.getValue<T>("alias")`. The theme looks the alias up in the Figma token map and turns the foundation name into a real value.

An old binder catalogue. First you check the sticky notes stuck on top (overrides). Then the index page (the token map) gives you a shelf code. The store room (CoreHarmonixTheme) turns that code into the actual tin. If the index doesn't list it, you ask the parent shop's binder (the parent theme).

items: **Overrides are raw values.** A Harmonix override is `"#FF0000"` or `"12"`, never `"{ref}"`. That is different from Lumen.
**Missing means null.** `getValue` catches the error and returns null, so every component reads `getValue<Color>(key) ?? fallback`. A missing token never crashes. It silently uses the fallback.

**No live updates.** `listen: false` plus `Provider(create:)` means a component reads the theme when it builds, but doesn't rebuild when a theme object changes. The `create` callback also runs only once for that provider element, so passing a new `theme` to the same provider later may keep the first one. Wrap with a **new** provider, for example with a new key, to apply a new theme.

blocks.text: On an existing Harmonix screen, stay in Harmonix. Use the component's own parameters first (`buttonType`, `buttonVariant`, `size`, `labelEnabledColorOverride`, or a custom `tokens: HarmonixButtonConfig`). For a section-level re-skin, the app wraps it in `HarmonixThemeWidgetContainer` with a theme built by `ThemeSettingUtils.getThemeModel` from `theme_json`. Don't migrate a screen to Lumen as part of a bug fix.
Four steps, and any failure becomes `null`. That is why Harmonix bugs look like "wrong colour, no error".

Lumen (`lumen`, pinned to `app_performance_improvement`, `aeb4da9`) has more moving parts than Harmonix. This chapter covers them in four steps: how a component is built, how a token is resolved, the two kinds of component, and the value formats. The component-by-component deep dives are in the separate Lumen guide topic.
26.1 · Anatomy of a Lumen component

Every Lumen component extends **`LumenThemedComponent`** and implements two methods. `createTokens(context, prefix)` works out all the sizes, colours and paddings into a tokens object, and `buildContent(context, tokens)` draws the widget from those tokens. Each component lives in three files: `X_enums.dart`, `X_tokens.dart` and `X.dart`.

A tailor. First take the measurements for this customer and this occasion (createTokens: size, variant, intent). Then cut the cloth from those measurements (buildContent). The measurement sheet is a separate page from the sewing.

Without a prefix, the stateless element calls `createTokens` then `buildContent` on **every** build. With a prefix, the stateful element caches the tokens and resolves them again only when the theme provider above changes (`didChangeDependencies`) or the prefix changes. The enums are the menu of choices Figma can make. If Figma shows something no enum allows, it isn't a standard variant.
To understand any Lumen component in five minutes, read in this order:

items: `_enums.dart`: what you can choose.
`_tokens.dart` `resolve()`: what each choice turns into.
The constructor in `X.dart`: which overrides it accepts.
The example file named in the Figma mapping rule.

blocks.text: One base class with two behaviours. Which one you get depends only on whether the component was given a `tokenPrefix`.
26.2 · How one token is resolved

**`resolveValue<T>(property, context, fallback)`** (from the `ThemeResolvable` mixin) turns a property name into a typed value. It builds the full key, checks a cache, asks the nearest `LumenThemeProvider` (which asks its parents), decodes the string it gets back, and falls back to `fallback()` if anything is missing.

A dress-code question at a wedding. Check your own table's note card first (the section provider), then the hall's notice (the page provider), then the venue's house rules (the root default brand). If nobody wrote anything, or someone wrote "no rule" (`"-"`), follow your own common sense (the fallback).

items: The **nearest** provider wins. Lookup goes up the tree and stops at the first map that contains the key.

A `"{name}"` value is looked up in the **semantics** maps (`SemanticsColors().map`, `SemanticsNumerics().map`, …), even though the class is called `LumenFoundations`. `"{bg-brand}"` works. `"{colors.brand.500}"` (a foundation key) returns null, so you get the fallback.
Decoded values are memoised app-wide per type (`_typedValueCache`, :36). In release builds a bad value is cached as null and quietly falls back every time.
With no provider above at all, it prints `[Lumen] No LumenThemeProvider found…` in debug and uses the fallback.

A mall where each shop front can hang its own banner and pick its own colours, while the corridor keeps the mall's standard look.

The server's map becomes the innermost provider. Anything it doesn't define falls through to the page and the root.

On a **server-driven page** (home, store fronts, dynamic pages, listings, PD) the server decides **what** appears and **in what order**, as a list of **sections**, each with a `section_type`. The app decides **how** each type looks. Loading happens in two phases. First the **layout** arrives (the list of sections). Then each section's **data** arrives in chunks, and a section appears only once its data is in.

A newspaper. At 6 pm the editor sends the page plan: "banner here, product row here, offer strip here" (layout). The typesetters set up an empty frame for each block. Each block's content then arrives from a different desk, and a frame is printed only when its content is in. Blocks the typesetters have no template for are left out.
There are **two switches** on the section type, in two different files:

items: **Switch A**, `BlocProvider.getBlocForSection` (`bloc/bloc_provider.dart:544`), chooses the section's **bloc**.
**Switch B**, `LumenDynamicWidget.getListItem` (`ui/lumen/widgets/lumen_dynamic_widget.dart:786+`), chooses the section's **widget**. Harmonix has its own twin in `ui/widgets/dynamic_widget.dart`.

A shop's light switches. Some are wired at opening time and fixed for the day (entry flags). Some are on a remote panel head office can flip during the day (growth config). A few are on a separate fuse box (Firebase Remote Config). Some notes get stapled to every order sent to the warehouse (the experiments header).

A new table needs three things: its create query in `AppDatabaseInfo`, a **bumped `databaseVersion`**, and an `onUpgrade` step. Without the upgrade, existing users already have a database at the old version and the new table never gets created. That crashes or silently fails only for upgraded users, never on a fresh install.

Flutter has three error doors. **`FlutterError.onError`** catches errors during build, layout and paint. **`PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError`** catches uncaught async errors, for example a `Future` that throws with no `catch`. **`ErrorWidget.builder`** decides what a widget that failed to build shows on screen. This app wires all three to **Firebase Crashlytics**, and in debug builds also to an on-screen error log.

A building's alarm system. Smoke alarms in every room (the error handlers) all ring at one control panel (Crashlytics). A blown bulb is swapped for an empty socket so visitors don't see a sparking lamp (`SizedBox.shrink`), but the panel still records which room. items: **Almost everything is non-fatal.** Build errors, async errors and manual logs are recorded with `fatal: false`. **Release hides the failure.** In release, the widget that failed becomes an empty box, so the user sees a gap, not a red screen. In debug, Flutter's red error screen shows instead.

lessons.title: M1 · What an animation really is

blocks.text: An animation is just **a number that changes every frame**, plus a widget that redraws from that number. Everything in this tab, from a fading button to the Rive basket, is a fancier way to produce that number.

Flutter redraws the screen up to 60–120 times a second. An **animation** is a value (opacity, offset, size, a Lottie frame, a Rive state) that is different on each of those frames, so the eye sees motion.
A flip book. Each page is a frame and the picture moves a little per page. Flip fast and it looks alive.
Every surface in this tab boils down to a value going from 0 to 1. The Free Cash sheet drives a Lottie's progress, the OT page drives a card's expansion, and the basket FAB drives a scale.

Something has to **tick** once per frame (a `Ticker`, given by `vsync`), something has to **hold** the value (an `AnimationController`), and something has to **redraw** (a `*Transition` widget, `AnimatedBuilder`, or a Lottie/Rive widget).
When an animation is broken, ask three questions: Is anything ticking? Is the value changing? Is anything listening and redrawing?
Every animation is a number that changes each frame plus something that redraws from it.
Widgets like `AnimatedContainer`, `AnimatedOpacity` and `AnimatedSwitcher` animate **by themselves** whenever a property you give them changes. You never touch a controller.
A dimmer switch with built-in smoothing. You set the level and the light glides there.
`currentPage` is fractional (1.4 while swiping), so the dots stretch smoothly as the finger moves. The 120 ms `AnimatedContainer` smooths any jumps in between.

blocks.code: AnimatedOpacity(opacity: isVisible ? 1 : 0, duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200), child: …)

blocks.text: Use it first. Reach for a controller only when you need staging, looping, reversing or a finger to drive it.

A controller is a **clock-driven number from 0 to 1**. `forward()` runs it up, `reverse()` runs it down, `animateTo(x)` stops anywhere, and `value = x` jumps (that's how a finger or a scroll can drive it).

`AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: …)` produces a value between `lowerBound` and `upperBound` (0 and 1 by default) over time. It needs a `TickerProvider`: `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` for one controller, `TickerProviderStateMixin` for several.
A stopwatch with a progress bar. Press start and it fills. Press reverse and it empties. You can also grab the bar and drag it.
A controller doesn't draw anything. It's just the clock. The Lottie widget reads `_lottieController` as its progress, and an `AnimatedBuilder` reads `_fadeController.value` as an opacity.
Use the four-place rule: create in `initState`, replay in `didUpdateWidget`, read in `build`, and release in `dispose`.
The four statuses. `animateTo(x)` and `value = x` let you stop anywhere in between.
The four places animation code goes, and nowhere else.

A **curve** reshapes 0→1 over time (fast start, soft landing, bounce). A **Tween** maps 0→1 onto real values (an `Offset`, a colour, a height). An **Interval** makes one part start late or end early on a shared timeline.
The curve is how a car accelerates and brakes. The tween is the route from A to B. The interval is when each passenger gets on and off.

In `Cubic(a, b, c, d)`, a **y value above 1** (like 1.58 or 2) means the motion shoots past the target and comes back. That's what makes the SKU counter and the basket FAB feel springy. Expand with overshoot, collapse without: this pairing appears in the counter, the OT page and the FAB.
Copy the curve constants from the design spec or a neighbouring widget. Don't invent them, because designers tune these numbers by feel.
Curves are the personality of motion. Plotted from the real cubic values in the code.

**Motion controller = one progress value that many properties follow.** Instead of five animations that can drift apart, you have one number, and everything else is computed from it with `lerp`. Drag, tap and timer all just move that one number.

A "motion controller" (the team's name for it) is the combination of an `AnimationController` (or a `ValueNotifier<double>`) holding a 0→1 *progress*, an `AnimatedBuilder`/`ValueListenableBuilder` that listens, and `lerpDouble`/`Color.lerp`/`Rect.lerp` that turn progress into every visual property.
A dimmer that controls the whole room: one slider raises the blinds, dims the lights and lowers the music together. Nobody can fall out of step.

The pill config splits one progress into phases (`phaseStretchEnd = 0.20`, `phaseMoveEnd = 0.68`). The pill first stretches toward the new tab, then its back edge catches up. It's still one number, just read differently by each edge.
Pass static parts as `child:` so they aren't rebuilt every frame.
The "motion controller" in one picture: one number, many synchronised properties.

blocks.text: **`LottieDelegates`** lets code replace text, fonts and colours inside the animation while it plays. A small **ChangeNotifier controller** lets any code say "play part X" without holding the Lottie widget.

**Lottie is a video you can scrub. Rive is a small program the designer wrote.** A Rive file has **artboards** (scenes), each with a **state machine** (states like idle, cheer, wave, and arrows between them). The designer exposes **inputs**, and code only flips those inputs. The state machine decides what to draw.
**Rive** (`rive: 0.13.20` in this app, pinned by both Lumen and Harmonix) renders interactive vector animations from `.riv` files. Inputs come in three kinds:

items: **Trigger**: fire once, for example "Hi" or "Add".
**Boolean**: on or off, for example "Entry".
**Number**: a value, for example a progress amount.

modules.title: Part 8: Dart language to Design systems and theming

blocks.text: Safe on the left, risky on the right.
What is the difference between `final` and `const`?

`final` is set once, at runtime. `const` is a compile-time constant, deeply immutable, and identical instances are shared. A `const` widget is created once and Flutter can skip rebuilding it, which is why the app writes `const SizedBox.shrink()`. Handbook →
What is sound null safety? What do `?`, `?.`, `??` and `!` mean?

Types are non-nullable by default, and `String?` opts in to null. The compiler then guarantees a non-nullable variable is never null. `?.` calls only if not null, `??` gives a default, and `!` asserts non-null and throws if wrong. In UI built from API data, prefer `?.`/`??`: a bad `!` crashes the build, and in this app's release build the widget silently disappears. Handbook →
What does `late` do, and when is it risky?

It promises the variable is assigned before first read, without assigning it in the constructor. It's typical for controllers created in `initState`. Reading it before assignment throws `LateInitializationError`. Handbook →
How do you write a singleton in Dart?

A private named constructor, a static final instance, and a `factory` constructor that returns it: `static final _i = Foo._internal(); factory Foo() => _i;`. The app uses this for `PageHandler`, `CartInfoService`, `GrowthConfigManager` and others. Note that in add-to-app with several engines, a singleton is per engine (per isolate), not per app. Handbook →
Mixin vs abstract class vs interface?

An abstract class is inherited with `extends` (one parent). Every class is also an implicit interface you can `implements`, which means re-implementing everything. A mixin adds behaviour with `with`, and you can use several. Examples here: `with ThemeResolvable` (Lumen tokens) and `with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` (animations). Handbook →
What are extension methods?
They add methods to an existing type without subclassing it. Harmonix uses `extension HarmonixThemeExtension on BuildContext` so components can write `context.harmonixTheme`. Handbook →
What are records and pattern destructuring?

Records are anonymous fixed-size tuples, such as `(int, String)`, and you can unpack them: `var (xTracker, cfId) = extractXTrackerIdFromResponseHeaders(response);` (`base_api_provider.dart:130`). Useful for returning several values without writing a class. Handbook →
What does the cascade operator `..` do?
It calls several members on the same object and returns the object: `_controller..reset()..forward();`. Handbook →
How does code generation work for JSON models?

Annotate the class with `@JsonSerializable()`, add `part 'x.g.dart';`, and run build_runner, which writes `_$XFromJson`/`_$XToJson`. Never hand-edit `.g.dart`. "Undefined name `_$XFromJson`" means the generator hasn't run. Handbook →
Widgets are cheap descriptions; elements and render objects do the work.
What is a widget?

An immutable description of part of the UI. Flutter keeps three trees: widgets (configuration), elements (the live instances that hold position and state) and render objects (layout and paint). Rebuilding widgets is cheap because only the differences reach the render tree. Handbook →
StatelessWidget vs StatefulWidget?

Stateless depends only on its inputs. Stateful has a separate `State` object that survives rebuilds of the widget. Use `setState` for local UI state, and a bloc or notifier when other widgets or the API care. Handbook →
What does `setState` actually do?

It runs your closure, marks the element dirty and schedules a rebuild on the next frame. It doesn't rebuild synchronously. Calling it after `dispose` throws, so check `mounted` after any `await`. Handbook →
Name the State lifecycle methods in order.

`createState` → `initState` (once) → `didChangeDependencies` → `build` (many times) → `didUpdateWidget` (when the parent passes a new widget) → `deactivate` → `dispose` (once). Create controllers in `initState` and release them in `dispose`. Handbook →
What is `BuildContext`?

The element's handle, its position in the tree. Lookups such as `Theme.of(context)` walk up from it. Never use a context after an `await` without checking `mounted`, because the widget may be gone. Handbook →
What is an InheritedWidget, and how is InheritedModel different?

An InheritedWidget shares data down the tree, and dependents rebuild when it changes. InheritedModel lets each dependent subscribe to one *aspect*, so only those listeners rebuild. The app's `GlobalPageData extends InheritedModel<Aspect>` (bottom bar, floating basket, sheet…) works this way. Handbook →
Why are `const` constructors important for performance?
A const widget instance is canonical, so when the parent rebuilds, Flutter sees the same instance and skips that subtree. Handbook →
What happens when a widget's build throws?

`FlutterError.onError` is called and `ErrorWidget.builder` decides what renders. Debug shows the red screen. In this app's release build the handler records a **fatal** to Crashlytics and returns `SizedBox.shrink()`, so the widget just vanishes. Handbook →
The layout answer in one line.
Explain "constraints go down, sizes go up, parent sets position".

A parent passes min/max constraints to each child. The child chooses a size within them and reports it up. The parent then positions the child. Most layout bugs are a child getting unbounded or too-tight constraints. Handbook →
How do you fix "A RenderFlex overflowed"?
A Row or Column's children are bigger than the space. Wrap the flexible child in `Expanded`/`Flexible`, let text wrap or ellipsize, or make the area scroll. Handbook →
Why does a ListView inside a Column throw?
The Column gives its children unbounded height, and a ListView wants to be infinitely tall. Wrap it in `Expanded`, give it a height, or use slivers in a `CustomScrollView`. Handbook →
ListView vs ListView.builder vs slivers?

`ListView(children:)` builds everything. `.builder` builds only visible rows. Slivers let different scrollable pieces (header, grid, list) share one scroll. The home page is a `CustomScrollView` whose section rows are built lazily by index. Handbook →
When do you need a Key?

When items of the same type can be reordered, inserted or removed and keep state. Without a key, state sticks to the position, not the item. Use `ValueKey(item.id)`, never the index. Use GlobalKey for forms, navigators or reaching a widget's state. Handbook →
How do forms and validation work?

Wrap fields in a `Form` with a `GlobalKey<FormState>` and give each field a `validator`. `formKey.currentState!.validate()` runs them all. Controllers hold the text and must be disposed. In this app `LumenTextField` shows its red error state only through `validate()`. Handbook →
The order Dart runs things in one isolate.
Future vs Stream?

A Future is one value later, and a Stream is many values over time. `FutureBuilder`/`StreamBuilder` rebuild UI from them. The app's custom blocs push page state through a Stream (`BehaviorSubject`). Handbook →
Is Dart single-threaded? Does `await` block the UI?

Each isolate runs one event loop. `await` doesn't block it: the function pauses, and the loop keeps processing frames and events until the Future completes. Heavy CPU work, however, *does* block frames. Handbook →
Microtask queue vs event queue?
After each event, the microtask queue is fully drained before the next event (I/O, timers, taps). `Future.microtask` and completed-future callbacks go there. Flooding it starves frames. Handbook →
What is a BehaviorSubject and why use it for UI state?
An rxdart Stream that remembers its latest value and replays it to new listeners. A `StreamBuilder` that subscribes late still gets the current state immediately (`base_dp_bloc.dart:34`). Handbook →
How do you move heavy work off the UI thread?

Use `Isolate.run(() => work())` or `compute(fn, arg)`. The work runs in another isolate with no shared memory, and the arguments and results are copied. In this repo: `Isolate.run` for gzip in `GZipCompressUtil.dart:54`, and `compute` for GIF frames in `gif_first_frame_cache.dart:127`. Handbook →
How do you stop a stale async result overwriting newer UI?

Cancel the old request (Dio `CancelToken`, as the search autocomplete does), or tag requests and ignore late replies. Also debounce input, and check `mounted` or capture references before the `await`. Handbook →
Every state pattern is this loop with different names.
What is the BLoC pattern?

It separates business logic from UI. The UI sends events or calls methods, the bloc processes them (including API calls) and emits states, and the UI rebuilds from the states. The result is testable logic and a predictable UI. Handbook →
How does flutter_bloc differ from the custom bloc in this app?

flutter_bloc uses immutable events and states, `on<Event>` handlers, `emit`, and `BlocBuilder` (used only in a few `screens/` features, for example `NotificationsBloc`). The app's own blocs hold a **mutable** StateData, and you call `notifyDataChange()` to push it through a BehaviorSubject to a `StreamBuilder`. Handbook →
Cubit vs Bloc?

A Cubit has methods that emit states, with no event classes. A Bloc maps event classes to states, which gives traceability and transformers (debounce and so on). Choose a Cubit for simple state. Handbook →
When would you use ValueNotifier instead of a bloc?

For a single value that a few small widgets watch: a badge count, a selected id. `ValueListenableBuilder` rebuilds only its subtree. It notifies only on a new value, so mutating a list inside it doesn't notify. Handbook →
Provider vs Riverpod vs Bloc vs GetX: how would you choose?

Provider is InheritedWidget made easy, good for DI and simple state. Riverpod is compile-safe, context-free and testable. Bloc gives explicit event→state with tooling, suited to large teams. GetX is quick but implicit. In an existing codebase the main factor is consistency: follow the pattern already used in that area. Handbook →
How do you avoid rebuilding a whole page on every state change?

Split listeners: put `ValueListenableBuilder`s or selectors around small parts, use `const`, and use InheritedModel aspects. This app adds revision counters (`PageChangeAspect`) plus `PageStateSelector`, so a pagination emit rebuilds only the list. Handbook →
What problem do global singletons cause for state?

Hidden coupling, they're hard to test, and stale reads. Here `BlocProvider().dynamicPageBloc` means "the page on top now", so reading it after an `await` may hit another page. Capture the reference first, or inject dependencies. Handbook →
How a page name becomes a screen here.
Navigator 1.0 vs Navigator 2.0 / go_router?

Navigator 1.0 is imperative (`push`/`pop`). Navigator 2.0 is declarative: the page stack comes from app state or the URL. go_router wraps 2.0 with URL paths, nested routes, redirects and `StatefulShellRoute` for tabs that each keep their own stack, which is what this app uses. Handbook →
`go` vs `push` in go_router?
`go` replaces the stack to match the location. `push` adds a page on top. The app's `pushPage` uses `go` for the first page and `push` after that. Handbook →
How do bottom tabs keep their own back stacks?
`StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack`: each tab is a branch with its own navigator, and an IndexedStack keeps them all alive. Here routes look like `/0/productListPage/productDetailPage`. Handbook →
How do you pass data between screens?

Through path or query parameters for simple values, or `extra` for objects. This app puts everything (`pageName`, `pageId`, `pageBuilderParams`) in `extra`. A route opened without `extra` falls into a white-screen fallback. Handbook →
How do you control Android back / iOS swipe-back?

`PopScope` (formerly WillPopScope) to block or intercept a pop, and `BackButtonListener` inside routers. This app's tab shell decides: close the sheet first, then pop, else go to the Home tab, else leave Flutter. Handbook →
Say this chain out loud for any "how does an API call work" question.
Why Dio over the `http` package?
Interceptors, cancellation, timeouts, FormData/multipart, progress callbacks and adapters. This app uses one shared Dio with six interceptors. Handbook →
What is an interceptor? Give real uses.

A hook on request, response and error. Here they: time requests (Firebase), add headers and cookies from native, refresh a 403 token and replay, log failures, retry once on 5xx or timeouts, and save a curl in debug. Handbook →
How do you design the repository/provider layers?

UI → bloc → repository → API provider → HTTP client. The provider knows endpoints and parsing, the repository combines sources and is mockable, and the bloc owns state. Inject the provider into the repository so it can be tested, as `ReferAndEarnPageRepository` does. Handbook →
How do you handle API errors without try/catch everywhere?
Return a result type instead of throwing. Here `BaseApiProvider` catches everything and returns `BaseApiResponseParser<T>` with `body` or `error`, and the bloc checks those. Handbook →
How would you implement token refresh?

In an error interceptor: on 401/403, refresh once (guarded so parallel calls don't all refresh), replay the original request with `dio.fetch(requestOptions)`, and resolve it. Skip the refresh endpoint itself. This app's `ResponseInterceptor` does exactly that with a one-shot flag. Handbook →
Is retrying POST requests safe?

Only if the endpoint is idempotent, or the server de-duplicates (for example by an idempotency key). A timeout doesn't mean the server didn't process it. This app retries once on timeouts for any method and sends `x-retry` so the server can tell. Handbook →
How do you implement pagination safely?

Trigger near the end of the scroll, but return early while any load is running and stop when `page >= totalPages`. Set the loading flag *before* the await. Otherwise you get duplicate pages. Handbook →
200 OK but the screen shows an error. What do you check?
The model doesn't match the JSON: a non-null field missing, or a wrong type. Here the converter isn't wrapped, so a `fromJson` throw becomes an error result and a Crashlytics non-fatal. Handbook →
Nearest theme wins; nothing found means fallback.
What are design tokens?
Named design decisions (`bg-brand`, `space-lg`) instead of raw values, so a theme can change many screens at once. Lumen layers them: foundations → semantics → per-component theme map. Handbook →
How does Flutter's `ThemeData` relate to a custom design system?

ThemeData plus ThemeExtensions cover Material theming. Custom systems like Lumen and Harmonix use their own InheritedWidget or Provider plus token maps, so they can support server overrides and per-section themes that ThemeData doesn't. Handbook →
How would you let the server re-skin one section?

Wrap that section in a nested theme provider built from the server's map. Lookups resolve to the nearest provider first and fall back to the parents. Only components that read tokens through the resolver pick it up; in Lumen, prefixed components do and fixed ones like `LumenButton` don't. Handbook →
How do you migrate between two design libraries safely?

Run both side by side, put a runtime flag on a page-by-page switcher, and migrate screen by screen. This app does exactly that with `enableLumenFlow` (Lumen vs Harmonix page). The cost is that a fix must go to the version the user actually sees. Handbook →
A design token is missing for a Figma value. What do you do?
Don't hand-edit the generated token file. Use the component's enum or override parameter, or a scoped theme override, at the call site, and record the gap for design. Handbook →

modules.title: Part 9: Server-driven UI to Scenario questions (answer like a lead)

blocks.text: Two phases: layout first, data in chunks.
What is server-driven UI and why use it?

The server sends a list of typed sections, and the app maps each type to a widget. You can change layout and order and run experiments without a release. The cost is a big type→widget mapping, and unknown types silently drop. Handbook →
How would you load a long SDUI page fast?

Two phases: fetch the layout first, then fetch section data in chunks for the visible part, rendering each section when its data arrives. Prefetch the next chunk, and keep auto-loading if too few sections render. This app takes chunk sizes from config, default 15. Handbook →
A section doesn't show on the home page. How do you debug it?
Walk the gates: in the layout? filtered out? bloc mapped? data fetched? `canRender` (data present)? widget case exists in this flow? visible after theming? Use the log tags at each step. Handbook →
How do you add a new section type?

Add a type constant, a state class plus a bloc, a case in the bloc factory, a case in the widget switch (and any page-specific widgets), and the theme wrapper. Decide whether its data comes from the server or is built locally. Handbook →
Measure in profile mode before fixing.
How do you find jank?
Profile mode plus DevTools Performance. Look for frames over 16 ms and see whether the cost is in build/layout (UI thread) or raster (GPU thread). Don't measure in debug mode. Handbook →
What must never go in `build()`?
API calls, heavy parsing, creating controllers, or DB reads. `build` can run every frame. Handbook →
What does RepaintBoundary do?
It gives a subtree its own layer, so repainting it doesn't repaint its ancestors or siblings. Use it around frequently animating parts, such as the floating basket here. Handbook →
How do you reduce memory for images?
Cache (`cached_network_image`), decode at the display size (`cacheWidth`/`cacheHeight`), and avoid holding large lists of images in state. Handbook →
How do you avoid duplicate concurrent calls for the same data?

Single-flight: a lock or in-flight flag so the first caller fetches and others wait or skip, plus a freshness window. `CartInfoService.shouldCallCartApi()` does this with a `Lock` and a 10-minute staleness rule. Handbook →
The four pieces of any explicit animation.
Implicit vs explicit animations?

Implicit widgets (`AnimatedContainer`, `AnimatedOpacity`, `AnimatedSwitcher`) animate automatically when a property changes. Explicit ones use an `AnimationController` you drive, for staged, repeating or interactive motion. Handbook →
What is vsync / TickerProvider?

A frame clock for the controller, which also pauses animations when the widget is off screen. Use `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` for one controller and `TickerProviderStateMixin` for several. Handbook →
How do you stagger several animations?

One controller, with each part wrapped in a `CurvedAnimation` with an `Interval(start, end)` of the timeline, and a Tween for the value range. The header animation here drives three parts from one 750 ms controller. Handbook →
Lottie vs Rive?

Lottie plays designer animations (JSON) with no interactivity beyond play, stop and loop. Rive has state machines with inputs that code can set or fire, so the animation reacts to app events. Rive names (artboard, state machine, input) must match the file exactly. Handbook →
Every test answer fits arrange, act, assert.
Unit vs widget vs integration tests?

Unit tests check pure logic with no Flutter. Widget tests pump a widget in a fake environment and interact with finders. Integration tests run the real app on a device. Use mostly unit and widget tests, plus a few integration flows. Handbook →
How do you mock a dependency?

Inject it through the constructor, then create a fake with mocktail (`class MockX extends Mock implements X`), stub it with `when(...).thenAnswer(...)`, and check calls with `verify(...)`. The Refer & Earn repository test is a real example. Handbook →
What makes code hard to test, and how do you fix it?
Hidden dependencies: singletons, static calls, platform channels and `DateTime.now()`. Inject them (constructor parameters or interfaces) and keep logic out of widgets. Handbook →
`pump` vs `pumpAndSettle`?
`pump` renders one frame (optionally after a duration). `pumpAndSettle` pumps until no frames are scheduled, and it hangs on infinite animations such as loaders or looping Lottie. Handbook →
Plus async errors through `PlatformDispatcher.onError` and broken widgets through `ErrorWidget.builder`.
How do you catch every error in a Flutter app?

`FlutterError.onError` for framework errors, `PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError` for uncaught async errors (or `runZonedGuarded`), and `ErrorWidget.builder` for what a broken widget shows. Report all of them to Crashlytics. Handbook →
Fatal vs non-fatal in Crashlytics, and how does this app use them?

Fatal means the app crashed, non-fatal means it was recorded but continued. Here almost everything is non-fatal. The only fatal is a widget build failure in release, which also hides the widget. Network exceptions are ignored. Handbook →
How do you read a Flutter crash stack?
Find the first frame in your own package (`package:bb_flutter/`). Library frames usually mean bad input from your call site. Use the screen keys (here `page_name`, `slug`) to locate it. Handbook →
"setState() called after dispose()": cause and fix?
An async result arrived after the widget was removed. Check `if (!mounted) return;` after awaits, and cancel subscriptions and timers in `dispose`. Handbook →
From source to the two kinds of build.
Debug vs profile vs release modes?
Debug is JIT with hot reload, asserts and slow performance. Profile is AOT with profiling tools, used to measure performance. Release is AOT, optimised, with no asserts. Handbook →
Hot reload vs hot restart?

Hot reload injects changed code and keeps state, but it doesn't re-run `main`/`initState` or update changed const globals. Hot restart restarts the Dart app and loses state. Native changes need a full rebuild. Handbook →
What is Shorebird / code push, and what are its limits?

It patches release Dart code over the air. It can't change native code or assets in the native bundle. A patch applies on the next launch. Here `auto_update: false`, and the app checks once per launch. Handbook →
How do you handle schema changes in a local SQLite DB?
Bump the DB version and add an `onUpgrade` migration step. Without it, upgraded users never get the new table, and only fresh installs work. Test by upgrading an installed build. Handbook →
The architecture answer as one line of boxes.
Describe the architecture of a large Flutter app you know.

For this app: a native iOS host with a Flutter module (add-to-app, an engine per VC) and a MethodChannel bridge. go_router with a tabbed shell. A page bloc per page through a pageId registry. Server-driven pages built from typed sections, each with its own bloc. A shared Dio with interceptors behind repositories. Two design libraries behind a runtime flag. Analytics built in Dart and sent natively. Handbook →
How would you design feature flags and A/B tests on the client?

Choose a source and timing (at launch vs live), typed getters with safe defaults, bucketing (a user's bucket id matched against variant bucket lists, with full rollout winning), and an exposure event. Read the flag at decision time. Here entry flags are fixed per engine and growth config updates live. Handbook →
How would you design an analytics pipeline for a mobile app?

A typed event model, one send door, a screen context set by screen views, batched impressions persisted locally and flushed on page leave, and a whitelist mirror to a marketing SDK. Make adding fields a contract shared by both producer and consumer, because here native drops fields it doesn't know. Handbook →
Pros and cons of add-to-app versus a full Flutter app?

Pros: incremental migration, reuse of native login, payments and deeplinks. Cons: a bridge for every interaction, per-engine memory and isolate boundaries, two navigation stacks, two-repo changes (Android), and a harder debug setup. Handbook →
Structure every scenario answer like this.
"After paying, the order screen shows the old status." How do you approach it?

It's a return-from-native refresh issue. Confirm which engine and page is shown, check that the page's `onViewWillAppear` refetches, and check for stale singletons. Add logs on both sides and do one device run before changing code. Handbook →
"Back from a tab leaves the app." Where do you look?
The tab shell's back handler rules (sheet open, pushed page, home tab, previous tab index) and whether the page uses `PopScope`. Read the go_router diagnostics for the location. Handbook →
"Server sent a new colour but the button didn't change."

Check whether that component reads tokens through the theme resolver at all. A fixed Lumen component like `LumenButton` ignores theme maps. Then check the exact key, a semantic reference, and nearer providers. Handbook →
"Two orders created from one tap."
Check for a missing submit guard (button not disabled while sending), an automatic retry after a timeout (`x-retry: 1` in backend logs with the same X-Tracker), or a 403 replay. Handbook →
"Works on iOS, hangs on Android."
A channel method is missing in the Android host repo, so the Dart `await` never completes. Add the handler there, and use a timeout on the Dart side. Handbook →
How do you review a change an AI wrote for this codebase?

Paths first (core network, interceptors, base classes, generated files are red flags). Then size against the bug. Then new singletons, flags, channels or hardcoded copy. Ask which page version it changed, what pattern it copied, and how it was verified. Handbook →
